Something also to add. CPU's pre-fetch the next instructions from RAM to speed up execution.

When you have a jump in assembly output then the CPU must jump to another location and therefore has to dispose the pre-loaded next instructions. If you design for speed then you must always make sure that the mostly used code is in the first IF part. The less used code in the ELSE part. This can make your code harder to read but it is optimized for speed.

This article is insane. I actually thought it was deep satire until I became convinced it was probably real to someone.

Here's the top two conditions from the article in something like C:

//Print a statement if input integer inputNum is even.
if ( inputNum % 2 == 0 )
{ printf("inputNum is even\n"); }

//Print out whether input integer inputNum is even or odd.
if ( inputNum % 2 == 0 )
{ printf("inputNum is even\n"); }
else
{ printf("inputNum is odd\n"); }

In this case, inputNum is divided by 2, and the remainder is kept. This is the "inputNum % 2" part- the percent sign is the modulo division function in C. A number of different things could have worked here instead- inputNum could have been logically ANDed with 1, for instance (this would appear as "inputNum & 1"). Because the statement following the if is one function call, we could have left off the curly braces:

if ( inputNum % 2 == 0 )
printf("inputNum is even\n");

... or even the spacing:

if ( inputNum % 2 == 0 ) printf("inputNum is even\n");

Or used one of many abbreviated ways to test it. The important point is, the expression in the parenthesis is evaluated according to a set of priorities (of which modulo division is above an equality test), meaning that the input number is modded by 2, leaving 0 or 1, and then the result is tested for equality with 0. Once there is nothing left in a conditional expression to evaluate, the code in the if statement is taken if the value is anything except 0, and not taken if the value is 0.

This would let you do stuff like:

if ( inputNum & 1 )
{ printf("inputNum is odd\n"); }
else
{ printf("inputNum is even\n"); }

While nothing is wrong with this, it's not very pleasant to read, and unless what you are doing is related closely to bitwise operators, it's better to use more easily readable stuff.
